extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, and researchers interested in public opinion and media trust
extracted.subtask_description: Write/report a public-opinion poll story that presents headline findings about public attitudes (here, trust in media), explains methodology, gives subgroup breakdowns, and places results in historical and topical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust measurement categories (4-point scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gallup asks respondents whether they trust the mass media 'a great deal' or 'a fair amount' to report the news in a full, fair and accurate way, with additional response options of 'not very much' and 'none at all'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report results using these discrete categories (counts/percentages for 'great deal'/'fair amount' vs 'not very much' vs 'none at all'), and highlight major category shifts (e.g., record-high 'none at all'). Use the exact wording of response options when possible for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report headline/topline findings and story highlights
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead with the chief findings (e.g., '32% have a “great deal” or “fair amount” of trust in media’s news reporting; New high of 39% have no confidence at all').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include succinct bullet-style 'Story Highlights' or topline sentences that summarize the most newsworthy statistics before detailed exposition to orient readers quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide historical/trend comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare current readings to past results (e.g., 'ties Gallup’s lowest historical reading, previously recorded in 2016'; 'statistically similar in 2021 (36%) and 2022 (34%)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize the current number within the historical record and explicitly note statistical similarity or differences across years. Reference prior notable readings and explain their significance (e.g., 2016 context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report subgroup breakdowns (partisan, age, independents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give results by key subgroups: Democrats, Republicans, independents, and age groups (example: 'Democrats’ trust ... to 58%, compares with 11% among Republicans and 29% among independents'; 'young Democrats trust the media far less than older Democrats').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include partisan and demographic splits to show variation across groups and note trends or changes within those groups (e.g., Democrats’ trust down 12 points since last year).

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey timing, sample size, and population scope
rubrics_metrics.description: State when the survey was conducted and who was sampled (example: 'telephone interviews conducted Sept. 1-23, 2023, with a random sample of 1,016 adults, aged 18 and older, living in all 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always report survey dates, sample size, age eligibility, and geographic coverage so readers can assess relevance and timeliness of the findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Margin of sampling error and confidence level
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the margin of sampling error and confidence level (example: 'margin of sampling error is ±4 percentage points at the 95% confidence level').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these statistical precision measures for the total sample and note that margins differ for subgroups; use them when discussing whether changes are statistically meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling frame details and respondent quotas
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe respondent quotas and composition (example: 'Each sample of national adults includes a minimum quota of 80% cellphone respondents and 20% landline respondents, with additional minimum quotas by time zone within region').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report quotas and any weighting or frame rules so readers understand how the sample was constructed and potential coverage implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection method (random-digit-dial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how telephone numbers were selected (example: 'Landline and cellular telephone numbers are selected using random-digit-dial methods').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify selection procedures (e.g., RDD) and other contact methods to allow assessment of randomness and possible biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit statement of limitations and potential sources of error/bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that 'in addition to sampling error, question wording and practical difficulties in conducting surveys can introduce error or bias into the findings of public opinion polls.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include caveats about non-sampling errors (question wording, nonresponse, fieldwork difficulties) and avoid overstating precision; note where results are 'statistically similar' rather than definitively different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide access to full question responses and downloadable data
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer a link or reference to 'View complete question responses and trends (PDF download)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make underlying tables, question wording, and trend data available for transparency and further analysis (PDFs, data downloads, embeddable charts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed or link visualizations/embeddable content
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide charts or embeddable graphics that summarize trends and subgroup differences to facilitate reuse by media and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize findings with related measures and broader institutional trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate the poll’s results to other measures (example: 'trust in each of the three branches of the federal government is also low' and references to TV news, newspapers, and journalists' honesty and ethics ratings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate the specific measure within broader patterns of institutional trust or related survey findings to help interpret significance and potential causes.
